question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration
question.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)-6{e}^{-3x}=1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1+6{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+6{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+6\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+6(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =x-2{e}^{-3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
question.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=6{x}^{2}-5.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6{x}^{2}-5)\text{d}x \\  & =6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-5\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-5x+C \\  & =2{x}^{3}-5x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}-5x+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =2\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-5\int x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})-5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{2}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
question.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-10\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-10x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-10x+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =-10\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+Cx+D \\  & =-5{x}^{2}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

question.knowledge_point: Sketching the Solution Curves of a Differential Equation
question.problem: Which of the following shows some of the solution curves of the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{2x}?$
question.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-4\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4(\frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}) \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Sketching the Solution Curves of a Differential Equation
question.problem: Which of the following shows some of the solution curves of the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{3(x-1)^{2}}{4}?$
question.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{3(x-1)^{2}}{4})\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}\int (x-1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\frac{(x-1)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{(x-1)^{3}}{4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plot the solution curves by selecting different values for $C.$ The sketch below shows the solution curves for $C=-2,0,2.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
question.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}-2x={e}^{x/2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{y}^{′}=2x+{e}^{x/2}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x/2})\text{d}x \\ y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2{e}^{x/2}+C \\  & ={x}^{2}+2{e}^{x/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y={x}^{2}+2{e}^{x/2}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(0)=2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & ={0}^{2}+2{e}^{0}+C \\ 2 & =0+2(1)+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y={x}^{2}+2{e}^{x/2}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
question.problem: Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4=0$ given that $y(-1)=4.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int (-4)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-4x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=-4x+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(-1)=4$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-4\cdot (-1)+C \\ 4 & =4+C \\ 0 & =C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=-4x\,.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
question.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14011969/assets/2135f70f6703878d5f82d3524c890af08e194d7fdfbe92e97a5305d142f73779.png)

Consider the circle of radius $2$ centered at $(2,1)$, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(4,1)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(2,1).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Velocity and Initial Position
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=3{t}^{2}+2t,$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=15$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
question.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(2)=15.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =(2)^{3}+(2)^{2}+C \\ 15 & =8+4+C \\ C & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+3.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Velocity and Initial Position
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}t-{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-7$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{4}t-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(3)=-7.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =\frac{1}{8}(3)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{3}+C \\ -7 & =-\frac{63}{8}+C \\ C & =\frac{7}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{7}{8}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=1-6t,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2$ and velocity $v=4$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
question.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-6t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-3{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(0)-3(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=t-3{t}^{2}+4.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+4t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}-(0)^{3}+4(0)+K \\ K & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+4t+2.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position

question.knowledge_point: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation
question.problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x{y}^{2}}{x+1}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(\frac{x}{x+1})\cdot {y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x}{x+1}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation
question.problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y{e}^{x}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\cdot y.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
question.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\,$ for $\,|y|<1.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arcsin}⁡y & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y=x+C.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form

question.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
question.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{y}}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{y}} \\ \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2{y}^{3/2}}{3} & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+K \\ {y}^{3/2} & ={x}^{3/2}+C \\ \sqrt{{y}^{3}} & =\sqrt{{x}^{3}}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3K}{2}.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{{x}^{3}}+C.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
